extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; practicing scientists and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for how scientific communities adopt, evaluate, and judge paradigms and scientific progress; describes the features of scientific communities, conditions for paradigm choice, and measures of progress. Useful for assessing claims about paradigm shifts, scientific progress, and the professional practices that sustain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for paradigm adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Two all-important conditions: First, the new candidate must seem to resolve some outstanding and generally recognized problem that can be met in no other way. Second, the new paradigm must promise to preserve a relatively large part of the concrete problem-solving ability that has accrued to science through its predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty for its own sake is not a desideratum. A new paradigm seldom or never possesses all predecessor capabilities but should preserve much of the concrete parts of past achievement while permitting additional concrete problem-solutions besides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for paradigm shift / role of crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior crisis proves important: scientists who have not experienced crisis will seldom renounce the hard evidence of problem-solving to follow what may be a will-o’-the-wisp. A decision to embrace a new paradigm often must be made on faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis makes the community receptive, but crisis alone is insufficient; there must also be some basis—rational or not—for faith in the candidate (sometimes aesthetic). Early adopters often act 'in defiance of the evidence provided by problem-solving.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties and expectations of early supporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters of a new paradigm, if competent, will improve it, explore its possibilities, and show what it would be like to belong to the community guided by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must develop persuasive arguments and concrete manifestations (experiments, instruments, articles, books) that demonstrate the paradigm’s fruitfulness; gradual multiplication of such artifacts helps convert more scientists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for membership in a professional scientific community
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership features: the scientist must be concerned to solve problems about the behavior of nature; the problems must be problems of detail; solutions must be accepted as solutions by many; the relevant group is the well-defined community of professional compeers; appeals to heads of state or the populace in matters scientific are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of a uniquely competent professional group implies shared training/experience and a common basis for unequivocal judgments; doubt about shared standards would imply incompatible standards of scientific achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation from laity and peer evaluation as enablers of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Mature scientific communities are unusually insulated from the demands of the laity and everyday life; individual creative work is addressed to and evaluated by other members of the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This insulation lets scientists take a single set of standards for granted, focus on problems they reasonably expect to solve, and increase effectiveness and efficiency in solving those problems—advantages not generally available to professions that must answer to broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational formation tailored to normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific education relies heavily on textbooks until late graduate work; textbooks systematically substitute for original creative literature so students are trained to solve puzzles within the tradition the textbooks define.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This education is narrow and rigid but immensely effective for puzzle-solving within a paradigm and for generating crises; it is poorly designed to produce individuals who will easily discover fresh approaches (paradigm-shifters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of scientific achievement is the solved problem; progress is manifest in the increasing number and precision of problems solved by a community and in the growth of the assembled data that it can treat with precision and detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress is often evident during periods of normal science when a common paradigm prevails; progress may be growth in depth rather than breadth (specialization proliferates). The perception of progress is community-relative rather than necessarily movement toward a single objective truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of acceptance and conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: No single argument can or should persuade all scientists; conversion happens as an increasing shift in the distribution of professional allegiances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because scientists are reasonable, various arguments will ultimately persuade many, but persuasion is cumulative and social rather than singular; persuasive arguments are multiplied over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and locus of judgment in paradigm choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to choose between paradigms must be vested in the members of a special kind of community (the scientific profession); nonprofessional authority should not arbitrate paradigm debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nonprofessional authority were the arbiter, revolutions might occur but they would not be scientific revolutions; survival and growth of science depend on professional control over paradigm choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of losses and trade-offs in revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions entail losses: repudiation of past paradigms often renounces most books and articles embodying them; revolution can narrow professional concerns, increase specialization, and attenuate communication with other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists tend to be blind to these losses; historians often note the distortion that professional education can produce in perception of the discipline’s past. Assessments of revolutions should therefore account for both gains and losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconceptualizing progress (anti-teleological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific development should be viewed as evolution from what we already know rather than evolution toward a pre-set goal or permanent fixed scientific truth; changes of paradigm need not imply movement closer to 'the truth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting 'evolution-from-what-we-do-know' for 'evolution-toward-what-we-wish-to-know' can dissolve vexing problems (e.g., induction) and reframes what counts as scientific advance; do not assume teleology when judging progress.
